intro: A fragmentary anthology tablet (KBo 64.14 joined with KUB 41.17) of rituals against plague. It preserves the end of a ritual against plague in the land and in the army camp (CTH 424), in which evil is sent off on a donkey and food is carried out for the plague-god and his dogs (§0–7); the ritual of Uḫḫamuwa, man of Arzawa (§7–8); the second to fourth days of the ritual of Ašḫella, man of Ḫapalla (§9–11); and the opening of a ritual of Tarḫuntapaddu, man of Arzawa (§11).

sections.title: Ritual against plague (CTH 424), final part (its closing words open §7)
Ritual of Uḫḫamuwa, man of Arzawa (begins in §7; the end of §8 lies after a gap)
Ritual of Ašḫella, man of Ḫapalla (second to fourth days), followed in §11 by the beginning of the ritual of Tarḫuntapaddu, man of Arzawa

paras.en: […] word(?) […] … […] … […] … Afterwards … before […] … (saying): 'These — the bull, the ram and the goat(?) — […] go(?)! Eat your fill, and drink […]! Get moving […], turn yourself (away)! Go to the enemy's land! Into the land of Ḫatti […] (do not?) come […]!'

Afterwards they drive up a donkey, and […] he places [u]p on (it), and he speaks thus: 'The donkey has taken(?) […]! Let this one carry off the evil, and let it […] take it […]! But let the evil not come to me […]!' […] the donkey. […] they [dr]ive (it), and […] it into the enemy lands […].

[But whe]n they come back from the open country […], (if) plague has occurred afterwards(?), … […] the house. […] he takes(?) it away from the fire […] [st]raw […] he scatters (it) [oppo]site, and he breaks a little bread opposite. When evening time comes, he pours (it) [down] into a basket and carries it out of the house, while the woman chants (palwae-, a ritual cry) in the gate.

They carry it across and come away. And he speaks thus: 'See, I have brought [fod]der for you, the god, and for your dogs I have brought food.' But if the plague has occurred within the army camp, then they do likewise from each one's tent. The first day is finished.

On the second day he does not take the bull, the ram and the goat(?). In the land he again scatters a little straw opposite and breaks a little bread opposite. When evening time comes, he pours it down into the basket and brings it out of the house, while the woman chants in the city gate. They carry it across and come away. And he speaks thus: 'See, I have brought fodder for you, the god, and for your dogs I have brought food.'
On the third day they again break … . On the fourth day … […] then three … loaves […] … […] … […] … the ritual(?) […]

… a ram with […] b[lack](?) wool […]. And if the plague [has come(?)] from an enemy land […], they drive a ram (there), and […] they bind it at the border, and they speak thus: '[…] to you, the god, with a sheep to meet (you) […]. And you, whichever god has caused the plague, […]! Go to the enemy's land! To the lands […] …' But if there is continual dying in some district, then they drive a tapananda- sheep (meaning unknown) toward that district and bind it to a tree at the border of the district; and there too he speaks in the same way:

'See, I have come to meet you, the god, with a sheep. You, whichever god has caused the plague, turn yourself back, and do not come into the land!' Complete. Thus (says) Uḫḫamuwa, man of Arzawa: If there is continual dying in the land, and if some god of the enemy … has caused it, then I do as follows:

They drive up one ram. They twist together blue wool, red wool, […] wool, black wool and white wool and make it into […], and they garland the one ram […]. To […] they drive (it) forth […]. [Gap: the end of column II and the top of column III are lost; they must have held the rest of Uḫḫamuwa's ritual and the beginning of Ašḫella's(?).] […] … […] they brought away. […] … […] … let him take […].

[…] early in the morning, quickly […] [twelve] jugs, twelve cups (and) twelve thick loaves […] … they arrange, and they drive them to the open country, again to another place; and all this they carry along with (them). When they bring them to the open country, they arrange them down on the ground, and they cook them plain. They spread leafy branches beneath, and on them they arrange the fat, the thick loaves and a small bronze dagger. Then they fill(?) the cups (and) jugs with beer, and then I(?) speak as follows: '[…] quickly […] first […] […] … […] now […]' [Gap.] […] he offers […] … cooked […] he drinks three times […]. Second day [finished(?)] […].

On the third day, when it [grows light] early in the morning, quickly they drive up one billy goat, one ram and one pig, and in front (of them) they arrange three thick loaves and one bowl of beer; and they drive them again to another place. They spread out leafy branches and set the three thick loaves back on them, and they offer the billy goat, the ram and the pig to that very god (saying): 'Whichever (god) (has caused) this plague within the army camp […], let that god eat and drink, and let him be at peace with the land of Ḫatti and with the army of Ḫatti, and let him turn to (us) in favour.' They eat and drink, and they come away. The third day is finished.

On the fourth day, when it grows light, early in the morning, quickly they drive up one bull, one ewe and three rams — the ewe (one) to which a ram has not yet gone — ten thick loaves, one bowl of beer (and) one bowl of wine, and they drive them to the open country, again to another place. He offers the bull to the Storm-god and the ewe to the Sun-god, and they offer the three rams to all the gods. They spread leafy branches on the ground, […] the shoulder, the liver, the heart and the thick loaves, cooked […] the Sun-god of Heaven, the Storm-god and a[ll] the gods […] they eat, and they […] away […]. [New text:] [Thus (says)] Tarḫuntapaddu, man of Arzawa: [If …] …, then I do as follows: […] … silver; but gold and silver … […] beneath a basket I arr[ange] (them) […]. […] I drive a billy goat, and it to […] […] I bind. Then the princes and the lords […] […] they […] it into a basket together with […]. […] of the king comes, and he bows down behind (it), and [speaks] th[us(?)]: 'Whichever god has caused this plague — (your) anger (and) fury […] down into this billy goat […]! I have given you silver and gold as a gift (IGI.DU₈.A, 'tribute'); turn […] to me! And the enemy lands which … […] … […] to this land(?) […]' […] and an oven(?) […] I offer […] […] … […] … (he) offers […].
